--- title: "From Dataset to Biological Signature" subtitle: "The same pipeline, told twice — once for a machine learning scientist, once for a statistician. The disagreement is only in vocabulary, and both vocabularies are describing a selection event." author: "Ravi Kalia" date: "2026-08-27" categories: [Genomics, Statistics, Machine Learning, Bioinformatics, Python] tags: [gene-expression, feature-selection, elastic-net, stability-selection, leakage, golub, leukemia] image: "./cover.png" description: "Golub's 1999 ALL/AML data, run end to end: recovering the original designed train/test split from an unlabelled CSV, fitting a signature with nested cross-validation, and showing why the honest error rate is the hard one to get." jupyter: signature-blog resources: - cover.png - data execute: warning: false format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 3 code-fold: show theme: [zephyr, theme.scss] fig-width: 8 fig-height: 4.5 fig-dpi: 150 --- ![](./cover.png){fig-alt="Cover card reading From Dataset to a Biological Signature, over a solid purple background."} Two acute leukemias arrive at the clinic looking much the same. Both fill the marrow with immature white cells, both make the patient acutely ill within weeks, and under a microscope the blasts of one can pass for the blasts of the other. They need opposite treatments. Get it wrong and you give a toxic regimen that will not work to someone who has a few weeks to spare. Before 1999 that call was made by an experienced haematologist reading morphology, chemical stains and surface markers. It was good, and it was not reproducible between hospitals. Golub and colleagues asked whether gene expression could make the call on its own — and whether you could have discovered the two diseases without being told they existed. This post runs that question end to end, twice. The argument underneath it is one sentence: **a signature is a supervised object, and every number you attach to one is conditioned on the selection event that produced it.** A machine learning scientist and a statistician describe that fact in different words. Both descriptions are here, and they are the same pipeline. ### Two assembly lines, and a glitch on one of them The biology is worth two minutes, because it turns out to be what the model recovers. Think of bone marrow as a factory with two assembly lines running from a single stem cell. The **lymphoid** line builds B-cells and T-cells — the targeted, specific arm of the immune system, the sharpshooters. The **myeloid** line builds everything else: red cells that carry oxygen, platelets that clot, granulocytes that do the frontline brawling. An acute leukemia is a glitch that jams one line, flooding the marrow with immature cells — blasts — that will neither mature into anything useful nor stop dividing. ```{mermaid} flowchart TD S["Bone marrow stem cell"] --> L["Lymphoid line
B-cells, T-cells"] S --> M["Myeloid line
red cells, platelets, granulocytes"] L -->|glitch| ALL["ALL
lymphoblasts"] M -->|glitch| AML["AML
myeloblasts"] ``` Jam the lymphoid line and you get acute lymphoblastic leukemia, ALL — the commonest cancer of childhood. Jam the myeloid line and you get acute myeloid leukemia, AML, mostly an adult disease diagnosed at a median age near 68, and faster to strip out oxygen transport and clotting because the myeloid line covers more jobs. So the diagnostic question has a clean biological shape: *which line is stuck?* Hold on to that. It is what the classifier ends up measuring. ### The data, and who went to the trouble of collecting it The measurements come from Golub et al. (1999) at the Whitehead Institute and Dana-Farber, who ran marrow and blood from 72 acute leukemia patients on Affymetrix HU6800 arrays — 7,129 probes, one fluorescence intensity each. They were not building a product; they assembled samples from existing clinical archives to argue that tumour class is legible in expression at all. A decision made from this analysis is a treatment assignment: vincristine and steroids for ALL, cytarabine and an anthracycline for AML, for a patient seriously ill either way. So the interesting quantity is not peak accuracy. It is how much of the accuracy survives contact with a different hospital. I use the copy on Efron and Hastie's *Computer Age Statistical Inference* data page, cached in this post's `data/` directory so the render never touches the network. ::: {#setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Imports, plot style, and loading the cached matrices"} import warnings import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from scipy.stats import beta warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") rng_seed = 0 plt.rcParams.update({ "figure.dpi": 150, "savefig.bbox": "tight", "font.size": 9, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False, "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.25, "axes.axisbelow": True, }) ALL_C, AML_C = "#1D5C6E", "#C98A12" # The CASI matrix: 7,128 genes x 72 samples, column names carry the labels. casi = pd.read_csv("data/leukemia_big.csv.gz") X = casi.to_numpy().T # samples x genes y = np.array([int(c.split(".")[0].startswith("AML")) for c in casi.columns]) # The original Whitehead files, used only as a key: they carry the Affymetrix # probe accessions and the per-patient sample IDs that the CASI copy dropped. def read_golub(path): d = pd.read_csv(path) ids = [c for c in d.columns[2:] if not c.startswith("call")] return d["Gene Accession Number"].to_numpy(), d["Gene Description"].to_numpy(), \ d[ids].to_numpy(dtype=float), ids acc, desc, G_train, id_train = read_golub("data/golub_train.csv.gz") _, _, G_test, id_test = read_golub("data/golub_independent.csv.gz") truth = pd.read_csv("data/golub_labels.csv").set_index("patient")["cancer"].to_dict() print(f"expression matrix : {X.shape[0]} samples x {X.shape[1]} genes") print(f"class balance : {(y==0).sum()} ALL, {y.sum()} AML") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` expression matrix : 72 samples x 7128 genes class balance : 47 ALL, 25 AML ``` ::: ::: Seventy-two samples, 7,128 genes: a hundred times more things measured than people to measure them on. Every difficulty below follows from that ratio. ::: {#cell-slice .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="A corner of the matrix"} pd.DataFrame( X[:5, :6].round(3), index=[f"sample {i} ({'AML' if y[i] else 'ALL'})" for i in range(5)], columns=[f"gene {j}" for j in range(6)], ) ``` ::: {#slice .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
gene 0 gene 1 gene 2 gene 3 gene 4 gene 5
sample 0 (ALL) -1.534 -1.236 -0.334 0.489 -1.301 -1.683
sample 1 (ALL) -0.868 -1.276 0.376 0.444 -1.230 -1.642
sample 2 (ALL) -0.433 -1.184 -0.459 0.436 -1.326 -1.407
sample 3 (ALL) -1.672 -1.596 -1.423 0.193 -1.818 -1.744
sample 4 (ALL) -1.188 -1.335 -0.797 0.236 -1.311 -1.654
``` ::: ::: The values are not raw intensities. Each *column* has been standardised to mean zero and unit standard deviation across genes, and beyond that the file's own documentation says the gene-level transformation is "lost in time". ## The file on Hastie's server is Golub's two cohorts, stored backwards Golub's design had a feature that matters more than anything else here. The 72 samples are not one pool. Thirty-eight came from a single institution, all bone marrow, and built the predictor. The other 34 were collected later from different reference laboratories, on different preparation protocols, and included peripheral blood as well as marrow — a genuine external cohort with a real distribution shift, which is the only kind of test set worth quoting. The CASI file has no sample identifiers, so that split looks lost. It is recoverable, and worth recovering properly rather than guessing from label counts. Per-sample standardisation is monotone within a column, so it preserves the *ranking* of genes inside a sample. Rank each column of both files and correlate. ::: {#recover-split .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="show"} G = np.hstack([G_train, G_test])[:X.shape[1]] # CASI drops Golub's last probe ids = id_train + id_test golub_y = np.array([int(truth[int(i)] == "AML") for i in ids]) rank = lambda A: np.argsort(np.argsort(A, axis=0), axis=0).astype(float) Rc, Rg = rank(casi.to_numpy()), rank(G) Rc = (Rc - Rc.mean(0)) / Rc.std(0) Rg = (Rg - Rg.mean(0)) / Rg.std(0) S = (Rc.T @ Rg) / G.shape[0] # 72 x 72 Spearman matrix match, best = S.argmax(1), np.sort(S, axis=1) print(f"unique matches : {len(set(match.tolist()))}/72") print(f"labels agree : {(golub_y[match] == y).sum()}/72") print(f"worst true match : {best[:, -1].min():.3f}") print(f"best runner-up : {best[:, -2].max():.3f}") print(f"CASI column 0 -> patient {ids[match[0]]}; column 34 -> patient {ids[match[34]]}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` unique matches : 72/72 labels agree : 72/72 worst true match : 0.945 best runner-up : 0.884 CASI column 0 -> patient 39; column 34 -> patient 1 ``` ::: ::: Every column matches one patient, uniquely, and every label agrees. The weakest true match scores 0.945 against a best runner-up of 0.884, so the assignment is not close to ambiguous. It also settles the ordering: column 0 is patient 39 and column 34 is patient 1, so the file stores the **independent test cohort first** — the reverse of the conventional layout. Splitting this file at the front hands you Golub's held-out samples as training data. One caveat that no amount of downstream care removes: the per-gene transformation the CASI page cannot document may well have been fitted across all 72 samples. Per-sample standardisation is leak-free, since a column only ever sees itself. That other step is not. Everything below is conditional on it. ::: {#cell-fig-data .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Figure 1"} test_ix, train_ix = np.arange(34), np.arange(34, 72) probe = {a: i for i, a in enumerate(acc[:X.shape[1]])} mpo, ccnd3 = probe["M19507_at"], probe["M92287_at"] Z = (X - X.mean(0)) / (X.std(0) + 1e-9) U, sv, _ = np.linalg.svd(Z - Z.mean(0), full_matrices=False) pcs = U[:, :5] * sv[:5] # Pick the axes by what they actually carry, rather than assuming PC1/PC2: # correlate each component with class and with cohort membership. cohort = np.r_[np.zeros(34), np.ones(38)] corr = lambda v: np.array([abs(np.corrcoef(v, pcs[:, k])[0, 1]) for k in range(5)]) k_cls, k_coh = corr(y).argmax(), corr(cohort).argmax() fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.6)) for cls, name, col in [(0, "ALL", ALL_C), (1, "AML", AML_C)]: m = y == cls a1.scatter(X[m, ccnd3], X[m, mpo], c=col, s=28, alpha=0.85, label=name, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5) a1.set(xlabel="CCND3 (cyclin D3), lymphoid", ylabel="MPO (myeloperoxidase), myeloid", title="Two genes") a1.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8) for cls, col in [(0, ALL_C), (1, AML_C)]: for ix, mark, lab in [(train_ix, "o", "training"), (test_ix, "^", "external")]: m = np.intersect1d(np.flatnonzero(y == cls), ix) a2.scatter(pcs[m, k_cls], pcs[m, k_coh], c=col, marker=mark, s=28, alpha=0.85, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5, label=f"{'AML' if cls else 'ALL'}, {lab}") a2.set(xlabel=f"PC{k_cls + 1} (carries class, |r| = {corr(y)[k_cls]:.2f})", ylabel=f"PC{k_coh + 1} (carries cohort, |r| = {corr(cohort)[k_coh]:.2f})", title="Colour = class, shape = cohort") a2.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=7, loc="best") fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Left: two genes named later in the post, one myeloid and one lymphoid, separate the classes almost on their own. Right: the component that carries diagnosis plotted against the one that carries cohort. Class separates left-to-right and the laboratory separates bottom-to-top, on different axes — the nuisance variable has structure of its own.](index_files/figure-html/fig-data-output-1.png){#fig-data} ::: ::: The classes are nearly separable in two hand-picked genes, which tells you the signal here is unusually strong — remember that when the error rates arrive. The right panel is the warning attached to it. Diagnosis and laboratory load on *different* principal components, so the batch effect is not noise smeared over the class signal; it is its own coherent direction in the data. A ridge classifier trained to predict which laboratory a sample came from, ignoring diagnosis entirely, reaches 78% under cross-validation. Batch is a learnable feature, and a model will use it if you let it. ## For the ML scientist: the signature is supervised, the plumbing is not **What is the design matrix, and where does the domain knowledge sit?** Rows are patients, columns are genes, entries are normalised expression. All the biology lives upstream of that matrix — which probes map to which transcript, how intensities are floored and logged, how arrays are normalised against each other. That featurisation is assay-specific and does not transfer; rebuild this study on RNA-seq and the whole preprocessing stack changes. What happens after the matrix exists is ordinary supervised learning. The asymmetry is why genomics pipelines break when they are ported rather than when they are fit. **Is finding a signature supervised or unsupervised?** Supervised, and worth saying flatly because the field's vocabulary blurs it. A signature is defined *relative to a phenotype*. Strip the labels and you still have structure, but structure is not a signature; it is a pattern that might be disease, sex, batch, or the day the samples were run. Unsupervised methods do the plumbing: normalisation, dimensionality reduction, and checking that the dominant variation tracks biology rather than the laboratory — which is what the right panel above was for. The exception is real, and Golub's paper is why it is famous. Cluster first, discover a grouping nobody had a label for, then treat the cluster assignments as labels. That is class *discovery*, and their paper did both halves. Discovery proposes the phenotype; the signature is still supervised once you have one. **What actually ships?** A fixed gene list, fixed coefficients, and a threshold locked before anyone opens the test set. Not a model you keep tuning. Which is why the penalty is chosen inside cross-validation rather than by looking at the answer: $$ \hat\beta \;=\; \arg\min_{\beta}\; -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[y_i\,x_i^{\top}\beta - \log\big(1 + e^{x_i^{\top}\beta}\big)\Big] \;+\; \lambda\Big(\alpha\lVert\beta\rVert_1 + \tfrac{1-\alpha}{2}\lVert\beta\rVert_2^2\Big) $$ The $\ell_1$ term forces most coefficients to zero, which is what makes the result a short gene list; the $\ell_2$ term stops correlated genes being picked arbitrarily one-from-each-group. With $\alpha = 0.5$ the only free parameter is $\lambda$, chosen in an inner loop while an outer loop estimates performance — so the number below never saw the data that produced it. ::: {#cell-fig-path .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Nested cross-validation, and Figure 2"} from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, roc_auc_score, brier_score_loss Xtr, ytr, Xte, yte = X[train_ix], y[train_ix], X[test_ix], y[test_ix] Cs = np.logspace(-2, 1, 7) def enet(C): return LogisticRegression(penalty="elasticnet", solver="saga", l1_ratio=0.5, C=C, max_iter=3000, tol=1e-3, random_state=rng_seed) def screen(A, k=2000): """Unsupervised variance screen. Never sees y, so it is safe inside a fold.""" return np.argsort(-A.var(0))[:k] outer, scores = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0), [] for a, b in outer.split(Xtr, ytr): g = screen(Xtr[a]) mu, sd = Xtr[a][:, g].mean(0), Xtr[a][:, g].std(0) + 1e-9 Za, Zb = (Xtr[a][:, g] - mu) / sd, (Xtr[b][:, g] - mu) / sd inner = StratifiedKFold(4, shuffle=True, random_state=1) C = max(Cs, key=lambda c: cross_val_score(enet(c), Za, ytr[a], cv=inner).mean()) scores.append(accuracy_score(ytr[b], enet(C).fit(Za, ytr[a]).predict(Zb))) # Full-training-set path, for the figure and for the final penalty. g = screen(Xtr) mu, sd = Xtr[:, g].mean(0), Xtr[:, g].std(0) + 1e-9 Ztr, Zte = (Xtr[:, g] - mu) / sd, (Xte[:, g] - mu) / sd cv5 = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=1) path = np.array([cross_val_score(enet(c), Ztr, ytr, cv=cv5) for c in Cs]) C_star = Cs[path.mean(1).argmax()] print(f"nested CV accuracy : {np.mean(scores):.3f} (outer folds " f"{[round(s, 2) for s in scores]})") fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.2)) ax.errorbar(Cs, path.mean(1), yerr=path.std(1), marker="o", color=ALL_C, capsize=3, linewidth=1.5, markersize=5) ax.axvline(C_star, color=AML_C, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.3, label=f"chosen C = {C_star:.2f}") ax.set(xscale="log", xlabel="C (inverse penalty strength)", ylabel="inner-fold accuracy", title="Regularisation path") ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` nested CV accuracy : 0.921 (outer folds [0.75, 1.0, 1.0, 0.86, 1.0]) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Inner-fold accuracy along the regularisation path, on the 38 training samples only. Accuracy peaks at a single interior value. To the left the penalty is strong enough to zero out genes the model needs; to the right it is weak enough to admit genes that only help on the training fold. Error bars are one standard deviation across five folds, and they are wide — 38 samples do not locate this optimum precisely.](index_files/figure-html/fig-path-output-2.png){#fig-path} ::: ::: Nested cross-validation puts the predictor at 0.921 on the training cohort. Now lock it and open the external samples once. ::: {#external .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="show"} final = enet(C_star).fit(Ztr, ytr) selected = g[np.flatnonzero(final.coef_[0])] p_test = final.predict_proba(Zte)[:, 1] print(f"genes with non-zero coefficient : {len(selected)}") print(f"external accuracy : {accuracy_score(yte, p_test > 0.5):.3f} " f"({int((( p_test > 0.5) == yte).sum())}/34)") print(f"external AUC : {roc_auc_score(yte, p_test):.3f}") print(f"external Brier : {brier_score_loss(yte, p_test):.3f}") wrong = np.flatnonzero((p_test > 0.5).astype(int) != yte) print(f"the one error : predicted p(AML) = {p_test[wrong][0]:.3f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` genes with non-zero coefficient : 88 external accuracy : 0.971 (33/34) external AUC : 1.000 external Brier : 0.041 the one error : predicted p(AML) = 0.468 ``` ::: ::: **What did it find?** Thirty-three of 34 external samples correct, AUC 1.000, and the single mistake sits at $p = 0.468$ — on the wrong side of the threshold by three hundredths, not a confident error. Note the direction of the gap: nested cross-validation said 0.921 and the external cohort delivered 0.971. The internal estimate was *pessimistic*, which is worth flagging because the failure mode everyone is trained to expect runs the other way. The gene list is what closes the loop back to the marrow. ::: {#lineage .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Naming the selected genes"} lineage = { "M19507_at": "MPO, myeloperoxidase — the granulocyte enzyme", "M23197_at": "CD33 — myeloid surface antigen", "X52056_at": "SPI1 / PU.1 — myeloid master transcription factor", "M84526_at": "DF, adipsin — Golub's AML-high list", "M27891_at": "CST3, cystatin C — Golub's AML-high list", "M92287_at": "CCND3, cyclin D3 — Golub's ALL-high list", "U05259_rna1_at": "MB-1 / CD79a — B-cell receptor component", "M31523_at": "TCF3 / E2A — required for B-cell development", } hits = [(acc[i], lineage[acc[i]]) for i in selected if acc[i] in lineage] for a, note in hits: print(f" {a:16s} {note}") print(f"\n{len(hits)} of these annotated markers survived selection.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` M27891_at CST3, cystatin C — Golub's AML-high list X52056_at SPI1 / PU.1 — myeloid master transcription factor M84526_at DF, adipsin — Golub's AML-high list M19507_at MPO, myeloperoxidase — the granulocyte enzyme U05259_rna1_at MB-1 / CD79a — B-cell receptor component M23197_at CD33 — myeloid surface antigen M92287_at CCND3, cyclin D3 — Golub's ALL-high list 7 of these annotated markers survived selection. ``` ::: ::: Myeloid markers on one side, lymphoid markers on the other. The classifier is reading out which assembly line is stuck — it has recovered the lineage question, not memorised 72 patients. And among the genes it keeps is myeloperoxidase, precisely the enzyme the pre-1999 cytochemical stain tested for. The expression profile arrives at the haematologist's own marker from the other direction. That is the optimistic reading. The next section runs the same pipeline and asks what those numbers are estimates *of*. ## For the statistician: every coefficient is conditioned on a selection event Recast the problem and the difficulty changes shape. This is sparse variable selection with $p \gg n$: 7,128 candidate predictors, 38 training observations, and an assumption that only a handful matter. The estimator picks that handful and reports coefficients for it. Those two steps are not separable, and the second inherits the first. So a naive confidence interval on a selected coefficient is meaningless. It is computed as though the gene had been named in advance, when the gene is there *because* it looked good in this sample. The interval is too narrow and the p-value too small, by an amount that depends on the selection rule. The repairs are known and none of them is "use the same-data p-values": split the sample and do inference on the untouched half; condition on the selection event explicitly, as selective inference does; or construct knockoff variables that mimic the correlation structure with no real association, and calibrate against them. Multiplicity is the second problem, and a Bonferroni reflex does not solve it. The relevant guarantee at this scale is the false discovery rate, $$ \mathrm{FDR} \;=\; \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{V}{\max(R, 1)}\right], $$ with $R$ the number of rejections and $V$ the number of them that are false. The practical difficulty is that genes are not independent. They sit in co-regulated modules, so one upstream event moves fifty together and the effective number of independent tests is far below 7,128. Benjamini–Hochberg holds under positive dependence, but correlation makes the realised false discovery proportion highly variable around its mean — you can control the average and still draw a badly wrong list this time. Stated as stages, the pipeline the section above ran informally is: 1. Lock the estimand and the operating point before looking at anything. 2. Split, before any transformation touches the data. 3. Fit normalisation and any filter on training folds only. 4. Choose the penalty in an inner loop, estimate performance in an outer loop. 5. Check the selected set is stable, not merely optimal once. 6. Lock coefficients and threshold, evaluate externally once, and report calibration and intervals rather than a bare discrimination number. Step 3 is the one usually violated, and the violation is almost never deliberate. ### Leakage is the default because the filter sees the whole dataset The natural way to handle 7,128 genes is to rank them by a two-sample t-statistic, keep the top 50, and cross-validate on those. It feels safe: inside the loop the model only ever trains on the training fold. But the *filter* ran once, on everything, so the held-out fold helped choose the genes it is later used to score. Ambroise and McLachlan named this in 2002, and it reproduces in a few lines. ::: {#leakage .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="show"} def top_genes(A, lab, k=50): m0, m1 = A[lab == 0].mean(0), A[lab == 1].mean(0) se = np.sqrt(A[lab == 0].var(0) / (lab == 0).sum() + A[lab == 1].var(0) / lab.sum()) + 1e-9 return np.argsort(-np.abs((m1 - m0) / se))[:k] def two_ways(lab, cv=StratifiedKFold(10, shuffle=True, random_state=7)): once = cross_val_score(enet(1.0), Z[:, top_genes(Z, lab)], lab, cv=cv).mean() fold = [accuracy_score(lab[b], enet(1.0) .fit(Z[a][:, (gi := top_genes(Z[a], lab[a]))], lab[a]) .predict(Z[b][:, gi])) for a, b in cv.split(Z, lab)] return 1 - once, 1 - np.mean(fold) opt, honest = two_ways(y) print(f"real labels : filter once {opt:.1%} error | filter in fold {honest:.1%}") shuffled = np.random.default_rng(3).permutation(y) opt_n, honest_n = two_ways(shuffled) print(f"labels shuffled : filter once {opt_n:.1%} error | filter in fold {honest_n:.1%}") print(f"chance for this class balance : {(y == 0).mean():.1%} correct by always saying ALL") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` real labels : filter once 2.9% error | filter in fold 4.3% labels shuffled : filter once 7.0% error | filter in fold 33.2% chance for this class balance : 65.3% correct by always saying ALL ``` ::: ::: On the real labels the gap is small — 2.9% against 4.3% — and that is the honest result, not a failed demonstration. The ALL/AML signal is so strong that leakage has almost nothing left to add. The second line is the demonstration. Shuffle the labels so no signal exists at all, and selecting genes once on the full dataset reports 7.0% error: 93% accuracy on pure noise. Do the same selection inside each fold and the error goes to 33.2%, against the 34.7% you get by always guessing ALL. The optimism is not a small bias that scales with the signal; it is nearly the whole number when there is nothing there. Leakage is almost invisible in the regime where you do not need the estimate, and catastrophic in the regime where you do. ### A signature is a draw from a distribution of signatures Optimality on one sample is not reproducibility. Refit on random halves of the training set and record how often each gene survives: genes chosen for real structure keep appearing, genes chosen for noise do not. ::: {#cell-fig-stability .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Stability selection, and Figure 3"} rng = np.random.default_rng(rng_seed) freq, B = np.zeros(X.shape[1]), 100 pool = screen(Xtr) for _ in range(B): take = rng.choice(len(ytr), len(ytr) // 2, replace=False) if len(np.unique(ytr[take])) < 2: continue A = Xtr[take][:, pool] A = (A - A.mean(0)) / (A.std(0) + 1e-9) freq[pool[np.flatnonzero(enet(0.5).fit(A, ytr[take]).coef_[0])]] += 1 freq /= B order = np.argsort(-freq) for t in (0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.9): print(f"selection frequency >= {t}: {(freq >= t).sum()} genes") fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 3.4)) top = order[:60] ax.bar(range(len(top)), freq[top], color=ALL_C, width=0.8) ax.axhline(0.6, color=AML_C, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.3, label="cutoff = 0.6") above = int((freq[top] >= 0.6).sum()) ax.set_xticks(range(above)) ax.set_xticklabels([acc[i] for i in top[:above]], rotation=90, fontsize=5) ax.set(xlim=(-1, len(top)), ylabel="selection frequency", xlabel="genes, ranked", title=f"{B} half-samples of the 38 training patients") ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` selection frequency >= 0.5: 45 genes selection frequency >= 0.6: 33 genes selection frequency >= 0.7: 26 genes selection frequency >= 0.9: 12 genes ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Selection frequency across 100 half-samples of the training cohort, sorted. The dashed line is a 0.6 cutoff. Genes above it are labelled by Affymetrix probe.](index_files/figure-html/fig-stability-output-2.png){#fig-stability} ::: ::: Forty-five genes clear a 0.5 cutoff and only 12 clear 0.9. The 88-gene list is therefore not one thing: most of its members are interchangeable with a correlated neighbour, and a different 38 patients would have returned a visibly different list with much the same accuracy. That instability is not an artefact of the elastic net. Reconstruct Golub's own 50-gene predictor with the signal-to-noise statistic from his paper, $P(g,c) = (\mu_1 - \mu_0)/(\sigma_1 + \sigma_0)$, and compare it against the same statistic computed after the preprocessing his methods section describes — clip intensities to $[100, 16000]$, then take logs. ::: {#golub50 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Reconstructing the 1999 predictor"} def snr(A, lab): d = A[lab == 1].mean(0) - A[lab == 0].mean(0) return d / (A[lab == 1].std(0, ddof=1) + A[lab == 0].std(0, ddof=1) + 1e-12) raw = G_train.T P_raw = snr(raw, golub_y[:38]) P_log = snr(np.log10(np.clip(raw, 100, 16000)), golub_y[:38]) fifty = lambda P: set(np.argsort(-P)[:25]) | set(np.argsort(P)[:25]) g50_raw, g50_log = fifty(P_raw), fifty(P_log) print(f"Golub-50, raw vs his own log10 preprocessing : {len(g50_raw & g50_log)}/50 shared") print(f"elastic net set vs Golub-50 (log10) : " f"{len(set(selected) & g50_log)} of 50 genes in common") print("top AML-high probes:", ", ".join(acc[i] for i in np.argsort(-P_log)[:4])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Golub-50, raw vs his own log10 preprocessing : 32/50 shared elastic net set vs Golub-50 (log10) : 26 of 50 genes in common top AML-high probes: M27891_at, X95735_at, U50136_rna1_at, M23197_at ``` ::: ::: Golub's own top 50 moves by 18 genes on a preprocessing choice his paper mentions in passing. Against that backdrop the elastic net's overlap of 26 out of 50 is neither a failure to replicate nor a confirmation. It is what two reasonable selection rules agree on when the underlying object is this unstable. The gene list is an estimate, and estimates have sampling distributions. ## Closing: 34 samples cannot pin down an operating characteristic The external cohort did what it was supposed to do. Collected elsewhere, prepared differently, including a tissue the training set did not, and the locked model still got 33 of 34 right. That is a real result, and Golub's designed split is why it means anything at all. But 34 is 34. ::: {#closing .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Intervals, and what happens at a different prevalence"} def wilson(k, n, z=1.96): c = (k / n + z * z / (2 * n)) / (1 + z * z / n) h = z * np.sqrt(k / n * (1 - k / n) / n + z * z / (4 * n * n)) / (1 + z * z / n) return c - h, c + h print(f"external accuracy 33/34 : 95% CI [{wilson(33, 34)[0]:.3f}, {wilson(33, 34)[1]:.3f}]") print(f"nested CV, 35/38 : 95% CI [{wilson(35, 38)[0]:.3f}, {wilson(35, 38)[1]:.3f}]") sens, fpr_hi = 13 / 14, beta.ppf(0.975, 1, 20) print(f"\nspecificity 20/20, but 95% upper bound on the false-positive rate: {fpr_hi:.3f}") for prev, where in [(0.35, "suspected leukemia at referral"), (0.02, "a broader haematology clinic")]: ppv = sens * prev / (sens * prev + fpr_hi * (1 - prev)) print(f" prevalence {prev:>5.0%} ({where}): PPV could be as low as {ppv:.2f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` external accuracy 33/34 : 95% CI [0.851, 0.995] nested CV, 35/38 : 95% CI [0.792, 0.973] specificity 20/20, but 95% upper bound on the false-positive rate: 0.168 prevalence 35% (suspected leukemia at referral): PPV could be as low as 0.75 prevalence 2% (a broader haematology clinic): PPV could be as low as 0.10 ``` ::: ::: The point estimate of 0.971 carries a 95% interval from 0.851 to 0.995. A model that got 30 of 34 right is not distinguishable from this one on this evidence. Specificity looks perfect at 20 out of 20, but zero errors in twenty observations only bounds the false-positive rate below about 17% — and carrying that bound through Bayes' rule is where the number stops travelling: predictive value falls from 0.75 at the prevalence of a suspected-leukemia referral to 0.10 at 2%. Which returns to the sentence at the top. A signature is supervised, so it is defined relative to a phenotype *and* to the population you drew it from. Accuracy is not a property of the model; it is a property of the model applied to a population at a particular prevalence. Golub's predictor answers "which of these two leukemias does this patient have" for a patient who already has one. Point it at a screening population and the arithmetic above, not the classifier, decides what it is worth. ## References **Biology and genomics** - Golub, T. R. et al. (1999).
